transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood CSM), Carlos (Brightlane ML), Priya (Brightlane Infra), Liam (Brightlane CTO), Asha (Brightlane SRE)

Summary (auto): quick review of last week's pilot numbers, agreed retune parameters for continuous batching and per-replica concurrency, decided on next-bench run and handoff steps for runbook + SSO.
Topics: throughput numbers, queueing/backpressure behaviors, KV cache hit patterns, concurrency targets, burst capacity tradeoffs, pilot billing and next milestones.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): ok hey everyone thanks for joining on time um i'll kick us off real quick, purpose today is to review the tuning results from yesterday's run and agree on the next bench sweep + handoff plan.
[00:18] Carlos (Brightlane): sounds good thanks, just to flag we had a production-ish replay that peaked at around 3k rps but the tail latencies spiked, that's what we wanted to dig into.
[00:29] Jordan (Redwood SE): right, so i'll go over the bench artifacts, there's two things: continuous batching behavior and concurrency per replica. we instrumented p95/p99, tokens per second, and queue depth. note, the transcription may flip some names but the csvs are in the drive.
[00:45] Jordan: baseline run (no kv cache): single model a100, 4 replicas, with concurrency 4 per replica we saw stable throughput ~1.1k requests/sec, p95 ~410ms, p99 ~760ms. with continuous batching enabled and kv cache warmed we hit 2.4k rps with p95 ~320ms, p99 ~650ms.
[01:10] Priya (Brightlane): wow that delta is big — was the kv cache warm across all replicas? i remember some replicas were cold during the test.
[01:18] Jordan: good Q — cache warming was uneven, two replicas had ~80% kv hits, two had ~40%. that mismatch is what caused queuing and head-of-line spikes.
[01:28] Asha (SRE): that matches what we saw on our side, the replay has hotspots early in the window, some prefix reuse then long tails.
[01:36] Liam (CTO): what is our target SLO again? anything above p95 350ms starts to annoy product.
[01:42] Maya: right, your stated target was 350ms p95; today we have three candidate configs to hit that while keeping cost reasonable: 1) increase per-replica concurrency to 8 and run small batches -> good throughput, risk of increased jitter; 2) keep concurrency low (4) and add a small queue with backpressure -> better tail but extra complexity; 3) hybrid: dynamic concurrency with prefix caching affinity that keeps KV-warm replicas handling hot prefixes.
[02:10] Carlos: option 3 sounds ideal but how stable is the affinity routing? we've seen affinity make some replicas overloaded.
[02:18] Jordan: the runtime supports soft-affinity, it nudges new requests to likely-warm replicas but still load-balances; if a replica reaches its concurrency cap it spills over. the important thing is setting queue depth and max concurrency per replica together.
[02:32] Jordan: in the last test we tried concurrency=6, max batch size=24, queue depth=48 and observed throughput 2.0k rps but p95 crept to 370ms during a cold-start window. p99 got noisy when the kv hit rate dipped under 50%.
[02:48] Priya: can you repeat that with sequence length shading? our logs show 70% of requests are short (<=128 tokens) but 10% are long (>=1024) and those long ones blow up the latency.
[02:58] Jordan: yes we included that in the artifacts; the long tails were primarily due to long-seq requests occupying the batch for multiple steps. continuous batching helps by grouping short ones together but still, long ones cause jitter. we can route long requests to a separate model variant (quantized) to maintain p95 for short requests.
[03:18] Carlos: that tradeoff would increase operational complexity and maybe cost for dual model serving. what's the estimated cost delta?
[03:26] Maya: quick napkin math from the pilot: single model baseline cost X, adding a quantized fallback for longs was about ~15% extra vCPU/GPU cost but reduced p95 for short path by ~40% and reduced client-perceived errors. i'll send numbers.
[03:38] Liam: send them yes.
[03:40] Evan (CSM): note we also measured token-level cost in the bench, Jordan can share the token/sec and token-per-request csvs in the folder.
[03:50] Jordan: ok next, backpressure behavior: when the queue depth exceeded 100 we saw automatic client throttling trigger in the pilot harness which dropped a small % of requests; that prevented meltdown but created user errors in the replay. if you prefer zero dropped requests we can allow larger queues but that increases p99.
[04:08] Priya: what's the expected memory/KV footprint when we raise queue depth versus increasing concurrency? we're constrained on GPU memory in your dedicated pool.
[04:16] Jordan: raising concurrency increases KV cache duplication pressure — more replicas hold overlapping KV segments. larger queues mostly affect CPU / request buffering and can increase latency but don't increase KV memory as much. so with limited GPU memory we recommend keeping concurrency modest and using smart batching + affinity.
[04:36] Carlos: okay so recommended default: concurrency 6, max batch 24, queue depth 60, affinity soft, kv prewarm for top 10% prefixes. does that sound right?
[04:47] Jordan: yes that's our starting point. In the 03/11 bench we validated that config gives ~2.2k rps with p95 ~340ms when kv warm fraction >70%. If kv warm fraction drops to 40% p95 jumps to ~420ms.
[05:06] Asha: what's the plan to keep KV warm in the pilot? we don't want to introduce constant synthetic traffic.
[05:12] Jordan: two options: scheduled prewarm windows (low-cost background requests to warm top prefixes) or sticky routing based on recent usage with TTL on kv entries. prewarm is simpler for pilot.
[05:22] Priya: we'll be ok with prewarm during our peak hours if it solves it. can you estimate prewarm cost?
[05:28] Maya: short answer: small compared to model serving cost, probably <5% overhead if targeted. we'll quantify in the doc.
[05:36] Carlos: also, what about burst capacity — we saw a rare spike up to 3.2k rps from a marketing campaign test, can Redwood handle fallbacks?
[05:44] Jordan: yes, there's automated fallback policy: during capacity pressure we route to a compatible quantized model (lower cost) or to a region-level fallback. burst capacity (on Redwood Dedicated) can be configured to allow short-term overcommit, but noted in pilot it needs a separate billing line.
[06:00] Liam: pricing line please.
[06:02] Maya: i'll include burst capacity tiers in the pricing sheet and examples based on the 3.2k spike.
[06:08] Evan: quick note on security/compliance — Priya and Asha asked about audit logs and KMS rotation during the pilot?
[06:14] Priya: yes we need KMS integration and audit logs to pass internal review for production pilots, any blockers?
[06:20] Jordan: no blockers; we support KMS + HSM integrations for Private/Dedicated. audit logs are available in the console; i'll attach the SOC/ISO snippet.
[06:30] Asha: also SSO, SAML for our engineers — can you do a run-through next week?
[06:34] Evan: noted, we'll set up a SSO walkthrough with Maya and me.
[06:38] Maya: ok going back to tuning, if you want zero dropped requests and p95 <350ms for short-seqs the practical config is: route long-seqs to quantized fallback, concurrency 6 short-path replicas, continuous batching max size 24, queue depth 60, and prewarm TTL 12 hours for top prefixes. cost increase estimate ~12-18%.
[06:58] Carlos: acceptable for now. let's run two bench sweeps: 1) validation sweep with your recommended defaults; 2) stress sweep with artificial burst to 4k rps and measure drop vs fallback.
[07:08] Jordan: got it. we'll run validation sweep first (non-destructive) and upload results. one caveat: our microbench harness slightly overestimates p99 compared to your production replay — there are environmental differences.
[07:20] Priya: understood, we'll supply the replay again with slightly more warmup to reduce variance.
[07:26] Jordan: perfect. any open technical unknowns?
[07:30] Carlos: just one — network egress spikes during peak, does Redwood observe any networking throttles in Dedicated?
[07:36] Jordan: not typically; Dedicated pools have tuned network bandwidth per GPU instance but if you have tight egress limits we can preserve a local deployment or adjust routing. we'll add a note in the runbook.
[07:47] Maya: quick check on timelines — Jordan, can you have the validation bench artifacts by end of day 2026-03-15?
[07:54] Jordan: yes, i'll run the sweep and drop the CSVs and flamegraphs by then.
[08:00] Maya: Maya to send pricing and burst tiers by 2026-03-14. Evan will schedule runbook + SSO walkthrough for week of 2026-03-23.
[08:10] Asha: one more ops question — alerting thresholds? what should we set in our pager for early warnings vs full escalations?
[08:16] Jordan: suggestion: warning at p95 >300ms or queue depth >40% of configured max; escalate at p95 >400ms or dropped request rate >1%. we'll put these in recommended alerts.
[08:28] Carlos: thanks.
[08:30] Maya: ok let's recap and finish with explicit next steps.

Recap / Next steps:
- Jordan to run 2 bench sweeps (validation + stress) with recommended config and upload artifacts by 2026-03-18.
- Maya to send updated pricing including burst capacity tiers by 2026-03-14.
- Evan to schedule SSO/runbook walkthrough for week of 2026-03-23.
- Priya to provide production traffic histograms and confirm acceptable prewarm windows by 2026-03-16.

Thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
